title: OpenAI Saudi national bugging case shows threat to U.S. leadership in AI: DNI Clayton
titleJa: OpenAI Saudi national bugging case shows threat to U.S. leadership in AI: DNI Clayton
summaryJa: AI "amplifies" existing cybersecurity risks toward U.S. digital infrastructure, Clayton said on "Squawk Box."
bodyOriginal:
U.S. companies and the Trump administration both "need to be wary" of foreign espionage attempts as the race for artificial intelligence dominance continues, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNBC on Friday.
AI "amplifies" existing cybersecurity risks toward U.S. digital infrastructure, which is interconnected with critical systems related to everything from public goods to the national defense and global communications, Clayton said on "Squawk Box."
It's "why we're focused on hardening those systems" and using "our commitment to continue to lead to stay ahead of those nefarious actors," said Clayton, who leads a new White House AI task force.
Clayton was asked how concerned Americans should be with the threat of foreign spying in light of the recently revealed case charging Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan with allegedly installing a recording device in an OpenAI executive conference room. Alfozan has not been charged with espionage; the federal charge involves alleged interception of oral communications.
Alfozan, who was an OpenAI employee, had booked a one-way plane ticket to Saudi Arabia with his wife and another family member prior to his arrest, according to federal prosecutors.
"The short answer to your question is espionage, both commercial espionage, and I would say state-sponsored espionage, are realities," Clayton said.
"It's something that our private sector companies need to be wary of. We, as a government, need to be wary of," he said.
The OpenAI incident "shows the lengths that people will go to try and supplant our leadership in this, or at least stay close to us in this emerging technology," Clayton said.
An ex-CIA official, who asked not to be named because they were discussing information that is not public, told CNBC this week that the case is "probably the tip of the iceberg."
Clayton, who was appointed AI czar earlier this month, said that the task force's "very good" inaugural meeting at the White House on Thursday built on the accord signed by President Donald Trump and a number of AI leaders at the White House last month. Trump had described the agreement, which includes industry pledges to police AI risks itself, as "morally binding."
The task force also established three subcommittees that are focused on different AI-related issues. One is tasked with reporting and response, another with assessing critical infrastructure and working with the private sector, and a third with law enforcement and responsibility, Clayton said.
The DNI reiterated to CNBC that the Trump administration is intent on staying ahead in the AI race.
"We're not the only ones developing it. There are vectors in this technology that are coming from some of our known adversaries and competitors," he said. "The Chinese, the Russians, the Iranians, the North Koreans all have significant technical capability. We need to stay ahead of them."

title: Analysis: Everyone expects the Fed to hold rates in October. Kevin Warsh could surprise us all
titleJa: Analysis: Everyone expects the Fed to hold rates in October. Kevin Warsh could surprise us all
summaryJa: Investors expect the Fed to pause rate hikes in October, but Kevin Warsh's rejection of traditional communications practices and continued concern about inflation leave the decision uncertain.
bodyOriginal:
Traders are betting overwhelmingly that the Federal Reserve won't raise interest rates when it meets later this month. But that judgment rests in part on assumptions about how the Fed communicates that may no longer hold under its new chairman. Kevin Warsh has left room to maneuver toward a hike, should he choose to use it.
To be clear, Warsh said outright at an International Monetary Fund event in Bangkok Friday morning that he wasn't signaling a decision one way or the other. His remarks nonetheless reinforced a judgment in the markets that the Fed would pause its rate increases, with the futures market assigning a 15% probability to an October hike as of Friday morning. That judgment follows remarks by other Fed speakers, including the chair's traditional top lieutenants, who indicated they were comfortable holding.
There are good reasons for investors to expect the Fed to wait. But there is also a case in the inflation data that Warsh could invoke to push the Federal Open Market Committee toward an increase on Oct. 28. Investors are overlooking that case based on longstanding past experience with the Fed.
But the chairman has repeatedly rejected the convention of telling markets what he plans to do before the committee meets. That raises the possibility that investors are dangerously complacent about the probability of a rate hike in October.
That complacency rests on a few bases. One is that the chairman's top lieutenants speak for him, or at least wouldn't contradict him in public. That was true in the past, but may not be so anymore.
In recent weeks, both Fed Vice Chairman Philip Jefferson and New York Fed President John Williams gave remarks that indicated they see little urgency in raising interest rates. The markets quickly repriced in favor of a hold in October.
Warsh, Jefferson and Williams make up an informal decision-making team atop the Fed known as the troika. Warsh could arguably coordinate with the troika even if he doesn't believe in communicating his own views. But outsiders can't be certain that traditional conventions surrounding the public statements of the New York Fed president and the Fed vice chair have survived the leadership transition.
Another assumption is that Warsh broadly accepts the FOMC's view of the economy. "The world has broadly conformed to our expectations," Warsh said in Bangkok of the economy since September.
That can be read as saying that relatively hot inflation readings from the consumer and producer price indexes in recent days don't disconfirm the view expressed in the Fed's most recent Summary of Economic Projections released at the conclusion of the September meeting. At the time, the median Fed official believed there would be one more rate hike in 2026 — which left room to pause in October and raise again in December.
But Warsh went out of his way at the September press conference to disclaim the SEP. "Those aren't my forecasts," he told a reporter.
Warsh set out his own idiosyncratic reading of the economy in detail at a closely watched speech in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, at the end of August. It described the economy as growing strongly, with inflation a greater worry than the jobs market. Warsh's strongly hawkish views then set up the FOMC to unanimously raise interest rates in September. That hawkish position relied heavily on what he sees as loose credit conditions.
The Chicago Fed's National Financial Conditions Index has risen about 0.05 points since Jackson Hole but remains negative, indicating financial conditions have tightened but remain loose overall.
Does Warsh believe the market has done his work for him? Is having "removed a dose of accommodation," as he put it Thursday, enough? We can infer these answers, but we won't really know them until the FOMC press conference.
Then there is the inflation data. The consumer price index rose 3.7% for the year through September, while the producer price index gained 6.3%. The new data implies that the next reading of the Fed's preferred inflation reading, core personal consumption expenditures, will come in at 3.1% year over year. Headline PCE, which will be affected by energy prices, would be higher.
Warsh has gone out of his way to say that figures at that level are a problem. After economists questioned whether Warsh might tolerate inflation above 2%, he was unequivocal in Jackson Hole: "There should be no misunderstanding," Warsh said. The Fed's 2% PCE goal "is a firm, fixed target."
Warsh is visibly learning on the job. He may well be coming to understand that the Fed chairman can't operate alone and must rely on the staff and the rest of the FOMC to help him do his job. Likewise, he may discover that markets don't issue a clear signal independently of the Fed.
Raising rates while the markets strongly expect otherwise is a recipe for volatility. That factor has prompted interventions by officials like Jefferson and Williams in the past. A surprise decision after they were seen to guide the market could dent their credibility and make the Fed's decisions even harder to predict.
But how Warsh will settle these matters isn't clear yet. Warsh could go into the October meeting primed to muscle up wavering committee members based on booming demand for AI spending and warm readings in the inflation data. Or he could sit back and tack toward the middle of the committee once he assesses its views.
Warsh still has the potential to surprise us, and it's risky to assume otherwise.

title: Why Trump and the GOP's billion-dollar midterm blitz isn’t working
titleJa: Why Trump and the GOP's billion-dollar midterm blitz isn’t working
summaryJa: Trump-aligned groups and Elon Musk have poured hundreds of millions into the midterm election, but the GOP spending surge has barely moved polls or the map.
bodyOriginal:
A billion-dollar war chest was meant to be Republicans' great equalizer heading into a bleak midterm election environment defined by economic frustration, President Donald Trump's unpopularity and fallout from the war in Iran.
So far it hasn't worked.
From Labor Day through Oct 14., GOP groups injected more than $740 million into congressional races that will determine control of Congress, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data. That includes at least $220 million in spending from Trump-linked groups. Elon Musk has separately given another $276 million to Republican groups since July and helped boost the GOP's Senate Leadership Fund super PAC to a record quarter.
Yet with less than three weeks until the Nov. 3 Election Day, the spending blitz has barely moved the map. Democrats lead in FiftyPlusOne's polling averages across nine of the Senate's most competitive races – Alaska, Georgia, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, New Hampshire, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas – little changed from before the Republican spending spree. Minnesota was expected to be solidly blue, making its tight race a concern for Democrats.
And Republican political operatives and independent election observers CNBC spoke with say the money hasn't had the effects its magnitude would be expected to in voter sentiment.
Meanwhile, the broader battlefield continues to deteriorate for Republicans. Democrats are favored to flip the House and remain competitive in the Senate, according to the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter, forcing the GOP to burn millions protecting once-safe seats while abandoning former pickup targets.
"Money is an amplifier, not a magic wand," said Neil Newhouse, partner at Republican polling firm Public Opinion Strategies. "You can buy all the airtime in the world, but if the political climate is blowing 30 miles an hour in your face, ad volume alone isn't going to turn the weather around."
Musk flooding the zone
Republicans entered the final stretch of the midterm election with unusually deep pockets.
MAGA Inc. had nearly $416 million on hand at the end of August, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Across the broader ecosystem, major Republican organizations had roughly $1 billion available, eclipsing the $579 million available for comparable Democratic groups, according to a CNBC analysis of Federal Election Commission filings.
Then came Musk — after saying he'd be less involved in this year's election. The Tesla and SpaceX CEO has given more than $276 million to Republican groups since July, including $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund Republican-boosting super PAC and more than $76 million to his own America PAC, according to figures confirmed to CNBC by an America PAC spokesperson. Musk's known federal political giving this election cycle now totals roughly $366 million, making him the largest known donor of the midterms.
And Musk is far from alone. Nine of the 10 largest individual and family donor groups this cycle are Republican-aligned, accounting for 86 cents of every dollar contributed by the top 10, according to a CNBC analysis of FEC records.
"We are watching an unprecedented concentration and scale of political influence and wealth this election cycle," said Hilary Braseth, executive director of OpenSecrets, a nonprofit, nonpartisan group that tracks campaign spending.
AdImpact projects $11.6 billion in political advertising this 2025-2026 cycle, surpassing both the 2022 midterms and the 2024 presidential election.
Paying more for less
However, the size of Republicans’ financial advantage may overstate how much advertising that money can actually buy.
That's because much of the GOP's money, particularly spending by Trump-aligned groups, has arrived late and via super PACs, which can pay far more for airtime than candidates. Federal law entitles candidates to broadcasters' lowest unit rate during the final 60 days before a general election; outside groups get no such protection.
It's an edge for Democrats whose candidates have generally outraised their Republican counterparts.
In Dallas, for example, Democrat James Talarico's campaign spent about $2.4 million on local broadcast ads from Oct. 1 through Oct. 14, enough for the average viewer to see his ads about 48 times, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data. The pro-Ken Paxton Texas PAC spent about $7.8 million for roughly 81 views per viewer – more than three times as much money for only about 70% more exposure, according to the analysis.
Airtime has become so expensive that Paxton's allies have begun buying ads during national sporting events, calculating that reaching enough Texans through a national broadcast can cost less than buying across the state's local television markets, according to the Associated Press.
"R money advantage not what it appears to be on [the] surface," Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, who lost to Paxton in the primary, posted on X on Oct. 5.
Across the nine key Senate battlegrounds identified by the Cook Political Report as of Oct. 1, Republicans led broadcast TV spending in seven and outspent Democrats by 26% overall through Sept. 30, yet generated only 7% more airings.
To be sure, super PACs don't face the same pricing disadvantage on digital ads, where campaigns and outside groups compete on more equal footing. But broadcast TV still dominates political spending, with AdImpact projecting it will account for 48% of the 2026 cycle total.
Little movement in political polls
But the payoff from all that spending has been harder to see in political polls.
Despite more than $113 million spent on negative advertising targeting Talarico since the Texas primary, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data, a Siena College poll released Tuesday showed Talarico leading Paxton 48% to 44%, down only slightly from his six-point lead in September.
In Michigan, after more than $87 million in attacks targeting Democrat Abdul El-Sayed this year, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data, Fox News polling from late September found El-Sayed's favorable rating among registered voters up five points from its early August survey, while Republican Mike Rogers' fell four points.
Part of the challenge is diminishing returns on ads as Election Day nears. Political advertising experts tell CNBC that as campaigns repeatedly target the same small pool of persuadable voters, each additional dollar is less likely to reach someone who has not already heard the message.
"When an undecided voter has already seen 20 negative ads today, the 21st ad doesn't persuade them. It just gets tuned out," said Michael Beckel, money in politics reform director at Issue One. "Their eyes glaze over." Issue One works to reduce the influence of money in politics and has a board that includes former Democratic and Republican elected officials.
Still, some Republicans counter that topline poll movement is the wrong barometer. They say the September cash influx helped keep vulnerable candidates competitive as the political environment deteriorated.
In Texas, Republicans spent $121.5 million on the Senate race in September, up from just $5.5 million over the previous three months, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data, while Musk's America PAC added direct mail and canvassing. Republicans involved in the race said the picture could have been far worse without that support.
"The spending hasn't put Paxton ahead, but it kept a messy race and flawed candidate from becoming an unwinnable one," said a Republican operative involved in the Texas Senate race, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly about the state of the contest.
Maine offers another test. Republicans have poured more than $50 million into the state to support incumbent Sen. Susan Collins, nearly twice Democratic spending, according to a CNBC analysis of FEC filings. Since early September, FiftyPlusOne's polling average has tightened modestly, from about a three-point advantage for Democrat Troy Jackson in early September to roughly two points now.
From offense to defense
The clearest sign that the GOP's cash advantage has stalled, however, is where the money is migrating.
In April, the Senate Leadership Fund announced a record $342 million advertising program across eight states designed to protect the GOP majority and expand the map. Texas, Kansas and Nebraska were not among the states.
Since Sept. 1, the SLF and affiliated groups — according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data — have spent or committed roughly $180 million across those three states, all of which Trump carried by double digits in 2024.
"Outside groups are diverting millions into deep-red territory to build defensive moats, leaving pickup opportunities starved for cash in the final stretch," Beckel told CNBC.
But those emergency defenses have come at a cost, diverting money from races Republicans once hoped to win and forcing national groups to narrow the map elsewhere.
In North Carolina, the Senate Leadership Fund initially pledged $71 million to back Republican Michael Whatley. On Oct. 2, however, the group pulled most of its remaining ad reservations after spending about $32.8 million, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data, as Democrat Roy Cooper continued to hold a double-digit lead in FiftyPlusOne's polling average.
It's a striking retreat in a perennial battleground where Republicans have won every presidential and Senate election since 2008.
The same triage is unfolding in the House.
The Congressional Leadership Fund cut off spending this week for vulnerable GOP Reps. Thomas Kean Jr. of New Jersey and Mariannette Miller-Meeks of Iowa following grim internal polling. The group also shelved efforts to flip Democratic-held seats represented by Reps. Kristen McDonald Rivet of Michigan and Greg Landsman of Ohio. The spending shifts were first reported by the New York Times.
Those four races had already absorbed about $13.7 million in Congressional Leadership Fund spending through Oct. 14, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data. CLF is redirecting roughly $10 million from those races across 16 other districts, according to the Times.
The new spending includes the South Texas seat held by Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz, a district Trump carried by 18 points in 2024. De La Cruz herself won reelection by about 14 points in 2024.

title: U.S. raises Mastercard, Citigroup China market access in bilateral Bangkok talks, official says
titleJa: U.S. raises Mastercard, Citigroup China market access in bilateral Bangkok talks, official says
summaryJa: The U.S. raised market access issues for Mastercard and Citigroup in China during bilateral meetings in Bangkok this week, a U.S. Treasury official says.
bodyOriginal:
BANGKOK – U.S. officials pressed Beijing on market access issues for Mastercard Inc and Citigroup Inc during at least two bilateral meetings with Chinese counterparts in Bangkok this week, according to a U.S. Treasury official.
The Treasury delegation, led by Deputy Secretary Francis Brooke, held bilateral meetings with officials from the People's Bank of China and the finance ministry on the sidelines of the Group of 20 finance meetings and the IMF-World Bank annual gathering this week, the official said, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss the closed-door meetings.
The talks included market access for U.S. companies, including Mastercard, Visa and Citigroup, the official said, adding that regulatory approval was part of the agreement reached during the meeting between Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping during the latter's state visit in Washington last month.
The sideline meetings in Bangkok continued discussions on implementing these deals, the official said.
The PBOC, China's National Financial Regulatory Administration, China Securities Regulatory Commission, Chinese embassies in Singapore and Thailand, the U.S. Treasury Department press office and Visa did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment. Citigroup and Mastercard declined to comment.
The progress follows China's Oct. 13 approval for Visa Inc. to begin preparing a wholly owned domestic card-clearing business. Visa has up to a year to prepare before it applies for an operating license, the PBOC has said.
China has opened much of its financial sector to foreign firms since 2018, gradually lifting foreign ownership caps on services such as securities, futures and fund management. It still limits cross-border capital flows and has kept state-backed domestic players dominant in payments.
Mastercard currently operates yuan card payments in China through a local joint venture with NetsUnion Clearing Corp., which began operating in 2024. The pending approval would allow it to operate as an independent entity, the person said.
Citigroup — which has hired several dozen employees for its China unit — is seeking a wholly owned securities license to conduct A-share brokerage, underwriting, research and principal trading businesses in the onshore market, two people familiar with the industry said, requesting anonymity for discussing private matters.
One of the two people close to Citigroup said the bank planned to increase its China securities staff to about 100.
The bank applied in late 2021, and Reuters reported last month that approval could come soon.
Trump and Xi are expected to meet in person for the third time this year in Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in November.
"The move suggests the US-China trade environment remains benign, and Beijing is keen to keep up the momentum," said Dan Wang, China director at Eurasia Group.
Licensing U.S. financial firms is a "limited concession" on market access, she said, though it signals China is continuing to open up, and "this should marginally bolster investor confidence in Chinese assets."

title: Here's how the CoreWeave sell-off is affecting OpenAI vs. Anthropic valuations
titleJa: Here's how the CoreWeave sell-off is affecting OpenAI vs. Anthropic valuations
summaryJa: The spread is widening between AI leaders OpenAI and Anthropic as a sell-off in CoreWeave leads neocloud stocks lower.
bodyOriginal:
The spread is widening between AI leaders OpenAI and Anthropic as a sell-off in CoreWeave leads neocloud stocks lower.
OpenAI's valuation is down more than 4% the past 24 hours after briefly slipping under $1.5 trillion, according to perpetual futures pricing on decentralized exchange Hyperliquid. Meanwhile, Anthropic perps are up 2.4% over the same time period, recovering an overnight dip and indicating a valuation of just over $2 trillion.
Perpetuals are bets that never expire. They maintained by "deployers" on Hyperliquid's blockchain infrastructure that determine a funding rate for going long or short the futures based on a spot "oracle" price that uses third-party data like private funding rounds and secondary market transactions to estimate private-market prices.
Open interest, defined by Hyperliquid as the sum of long and short positions on a contract, is more than five times bigger in Anthropic than OpenAI — more than $41 million, compared to less than $7 million in OpenAI.
Right now the deployer behind these pre-IPO contracts – the developer building the exchange – is Entropy IO. TradeXYZ, the most prominent developer on the platform, typically does not list pre-IPO perps until S-1s are public, according to David Schamis, CEO of Hyperliquid Strategies, the publicly traded treasury company that invests in the HYPE token that powers the exchange.
"Liquidity will probably be deeper once TradeXYZ lists these companies," Schamis said in a call. "Generally these will trade at a premium to the IPO price but they do a good job predicting where it will be post-IPO."
The bigger price drop in OpenAI perps reflects the company's closer ties to GPU rent-a-center CoreWeave, whose shares touched a new one-year low Thursday, extending a decline over that period to 54%, as concerns mount over the company's debt-financing strategy.
In April, CoreWeave announced a deal with Anthropic to power the company's Claude products, but did not disclose the value of the deal. The company's relationship with OpenAI stretches back further, and as of September 2025 was worth at least $22 billion including a 5-year agreement to provide datacenters and technology.
While OpenAI perps are falling more than Anthropic the past 24 hours, the two are both down about 15% from highs last month, according to Hyperliquid pricing.

A new version of Tesla's Roadster electric sports car, equipped with thrusters which apparently allow it to hover and turn in mid-air, has been unveiled in Texas.

title: Nike's India campus is a long-term growth bet amid turnaround
titleJa: Nike's India campus is a long-term growth bet amid turnaround
summaryJa: Nike announced earlier this month that it's expanding into India. The retailer has been broadly struggling, especially in the China market.
bodyOriginal:
Nike is making a big bet on India.
The retailer, which has been struggling to revive its business and regain momentum under CEO Elliott Hill, is hoping the world's most populous country can help it turn the page on its performance.
As it reported its fiscal first-quarter earnings on Oct. 1, the company announced it will create a new global campus in Bengaluru, India, as part of its growth strategy. Hill wrote in a letter to employees that the new facility would be a "long-term investment" to help position Nike for success.
"India is already an important growth market and manufacturing hub for Nike, with strong capabilities and access to talent," Hill wrote.
The new campus is expected to open in the next few years and span corporate roles across the organization, including the namesake Nike brand, Jordan Brand and Converse. Nike plans to discuss its India campus in detail at its investor day next month.
In a statement to CNBC, a Nike spokesperson said expanding into India is a "natural" next step for the company as it looks to grow its global presence.
"As participation in running, basketball, football, fitness and other sports continues to grow across India, we see an opportunity to better serve athletes through stronger local capabilities, consumer insights, and innovation," the spokesperson said.
India will be the world's third-largest retail market by 2030, according to Indian conglomerate Reliance Industries. Its e-commerce market was valued at $159.25 billion in 2026 and is projected to reach $332.94 billion by 2031, according to IBEF, a business advocacy organization created by the Indian government.
Nike has endured a yearslong slump and is trying to right its business under Hill's turnaround plan. Nike also announced this month that it would lay off workers across the company as part of what it has dubbed its Pace strategy, which includes supply chain changes and reorganization of the company's geographic segments. Nike expects the effort to deliver approximately $2.5 billion in savings through fiscal 2031.
Nike's decision to invest further in India as part of its comeback comes as the sportswear company sheds revenue in another critical international market: China. Though its fiscal first-quarter North America revenue came in just above Wall Street expectations, Hill said that performance wasn't enough to offset pressures abroad.
Nike has been particularly struggling in the Greater China market, where its revenue dropped by 26% in its fiscal first quarter. It's part of what experts have said is a broader trend of American companies losing relevance and traction to domestic brands as the once-lucrative market matures.
On a call with analysts earlier this month, Hill said the company was taking "deliberate actions" to strengthen its China business, though he said those effects will take time to materialize. Hill said the company plans to refresh its physical retail, spearhead a digital cleanup and create higher quality experiences for consumers.
The Nike spokesperson told CNBC the company is "deeply committed" to China and sees the region as one of its "most important long-term growth markets," even as Nike expands its presence in India.
"China remains a long-term priority for Nike, while India represents another important opportunity to invest in the future of sport and the next generation of athletes," the spokesperson said.
Investing in a long-term vision
The company's expansion in India may be coming at both an opportune and inopportune time, according to experts. Investing in a growing international market does not guarantee higher sales — it also requires persuading Indian consumers they want the Nike brand, a challenge the company has struggled to overcome in China.
"What Nike, I think, is doing right now is going region by region and working to reestablish what the brand stands for," Simeon Siegel, a senior managing director at Guggenheim Securities, told CNBC.
Siegel said part of the dissonance for Nike is that each region and segment of the business is at a different stage of its turnaround. He said investing in India may set the company up for a more sustainable future if the China business continues to lag, but Nike needs to have a compelling product, solid storytelling and extensive distribution in the region to be successful there.
"I think the company needs to look inward and figure out what is the right way to reestablish profitability," he said. "And that involves, in certain instances, shrinking and saving and cutting, and, in certain instances, investing and looking toward the future, because the goal here is not to shrink to oblivion; it's to shrink to stability, and then ultimately growth."
The global strategy may also focus too much on a long-term vision rather than more immediate fixes, according to Jessica Ramirez, co-founder and managing director at advisory firm The Consumer Collective, who specializes in retail and apparel. Ramirez said she already thought Nike and Hill's vision were "out of touch" and the plan for the India campus didn't necessarily help its case.
"I don't know that this plan of India is an immediate solution to their problems right now," she said. "They have to plan long term, right? But they also need to plan short term, which is continuously falling apart."
She said Nike has not shared plans that are concrete enough to win back momentum in China and has to develop both regions hand in hand.
While Nike under Hill has improved its wholesale and performance categories, Ramirez said it has yet to master its direct-to-consumer and sportswear segments, which would allow the company to flourish in all of its markets.
The Nike spokesperson told CNBC the retailer is committed to investing in both countries as it tries to expand its global presence.
"Importantly, this is not an either/or decision between India and China," the spokesperson said. "We always invest market by market based on long-term opportunities to serve athletes and grow sport around the world."
A growing market opportunity
Still, India presents an attractive opportunity for many companies looking to unlock growth abroad.
Ramirez said Nike is just the latest to join a cohort of American companies looking to establish their presence in the market. While many brands began investing in China years ago, she said that trend is now pointing toward India instead, as U.S. companies see more spending pressures in the Chinese market and navigate geopolitical tensions between the two countries.
"It's to get in there for the long term and to make sure that they are there for when they can reap the positive effects," she said. "I want to say this conversation started getting a bit more engaging in the last two to three years, when companies started investing more in India."
India is one of the world's strongest market performers, driven primarily by domestic demand, investment and supply-chain diversification, according to an analysis from Accenture. With a population of over 1 billion, the country presents a growth opportunity similar to the one China offered in the early 2000s.
"It's going to be a fast-growing consumer base where we assume their income levels will continue to go up and they'll have much more purchasing power, and so maybe could we be tapping in on that market from a consumer lens," Chris Tomsovic, who leads Accenture's macro foresight team, told CNBC.
Still, one of the biggest focus points for the Indian consumer is price sensitivity, which will pose a challenge for American companies trying to break into the market, he added. Even so, many domestic brands on the market are younger, meaning there could be more opportunities right now for Western companies to take market share.
Another challenge is that the Chinese consumer has historically been receptive to American brands, whereas it will still take more data to understand how Indian shoppers feel about those businesses, he said. For sportswear retailers, the focus of the sports most popular in each region will also factor into that equation.
"Can they really localize the product, make the price point work? Can they adapt to the local social media technology ecosystem? Can they adapt to the local cultural values and norms that the consumer wants?" Tomsovic said.
"If you're able to nail that, then I think you're right. Whether you're a footwear brand, whether you're an athleisure brand, I think there's a huge opportunity there with a billion consumers," he said.

title: Norway's $2 trillion wealth fund was frozen out of major defense companies. That may be about to change
titleJa: Norway's $2 trillion wealth fund was frozen out of major defense companies. That may be about to change
summaryJa: Existing ethical rules mean the fund is not permitted to invest in companies like Lockheed Martin and Boeing.
bodyOriginal:
Norway's $2.3 trillion oil fund could soon invest in Western defense companies after years of being frozen out of much of the sector by state ethics guidelines.
The sovereign wealth fund is currently worth around 21.8 trillion Norwegian kroner, or $2.3 trillion, making it the largest fund of its kind in the world. With stakes in around 1.5% of the world's publicly listed companies, the fund is one of the biggest investors in the stock market worldwide.
In November 2025, a review was ordered into the ethical guidelines governing how Norges Bank invests, following controversy over divestments from some Israeli and American firms.
On Thursday, the independent Gjedrem Committee submitted the review's findings to the Norwegian Ministry of Finance. It included a recommendation for radical change to the fund's approach to defense investments, arguing that "Norges Bank must be prepared for situations where conflicts escalate into war."
Current ethical rules prohibit the fund from making investments in companies including Airbus, BAE Systems, Boeing, BWX Technologies and Lockheed Martin, as they contribute to the manufacturing of nuclear weapons. The fund does hold some defense stocks, including a 2.3% stake in Germany's Rheinmetall, and a 1.5% stake in Italy's Leonardo.
The Gjedrem Committee said Thursday that although the nuclear weapons criterion should be retained, "its scope should change."
"The Fund is not to be invested in companies that produce nuclear weapons, unless the company is domiciled in a nuclear-weapon state under the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) that is allied with Norway," it said in its report. "Several European and American companies that produce components for nuclear weapons can therefore be reincluded."
It added that potential investment should include companies producing weapons that Norway needs for its own defense, and proposed removing the requirement for arms-makers to be assessed for whether their products are being used by nations in accordance with international humanitarian law.
The committee noted that alongside rising geopolitical instability, wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, and energy security concerns, the fund's capital and influence meant it was "timely to reassess the ethical framework."
"The Fund's size and reach give better access to company management and boards than the Fund had in 2003," it said. "In a time of a more demanding political situation abroad, this provides opportunities of which the management should make use."
"The liberal, rules-based international order is in decline," it added. "Economic policies are increasingly used as instruments of foreign policy. Cooperation between countries has become more transactional and negotiation-driven in recent years."
It warned that in this environment, other governments can "more readily perceive ethically motivated exclusions as the policy of the Norwegian government."

title: Trump says he won't use nuclear weapons or send ground troops to Iran
titleJa: Trump says he won't use nuclear weapons or send ground troops to Iran
summaryJa: Trump said he would not use nuclear weapons against Iran or send ground troops as the U.S. reportedly weighs new strike options.
bodyOriginal:
U.S. President Donald Trump has said he does not intend to use nuclear weapons against Iran or foresee deploying ground troops in the country.
Speaking in an interview with Newsmax, broadcast Thursday evening, he said: "I wouldn't use nuclear. We don't have to. We're the greatest nuclear power in the world."
The right-wing cable outlet asked Trump about reports that Washington was considering using the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast, or MOAB, widely known as the "Mother of All Bombs."
"The mother of all bombs is not nuclear. It's not nuclear at all. This is just an extremely large bomb. It's like a tiny nuclear bomb. But the mother of all bombs is one big bomb, but it's not nuclear," he said, without specifically confirming or denying the reports.
When asked if he would put "troops on the ground," Trump said: "No, I don't see that, I don't see it."
The MOAB is the largest non-nuclear bomb in the U.S. arsenal. It was used in combat in 2017 against ISIS militants in Afghanistan.
MOAB strike plans
Earlier on Thursday, CNN reported that the U.S. military has developed new strike plans to target Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites.
The strikes could take place if Trump orders combat operations to resume, either before or after the midterm elections, the outlet reported. The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.
Trump said on Oct. 8 that he would not order a resumption of military strikes before the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
Hormuz attack risk
Merchant shipping through the Strait of Hormuz faces heightened risks after a series of attacks in the critical waterway.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said that the threat remains "severe" in the Strait of Hormuz, after the Singapore-registered container ship GFS Pride was struck by an unknown projectile, caught fire and later sank.
The UKMTO added that "deliberate hostile action" was highly likely and said it had recorded eight attacks in the critical waterway since Oct. 11.

title: Ship attack reports near Hormuz reach record high as oil exports slow
titleJa: Ship attack reports near Hormuz reach record high as oil exports slow
summaryJa: BBC Verify analysis of data from a UK maritime agency shows 12 vessels were struck in a week.
bodyOriginal:
Ship attack reports near Hormuz reach record high as oil exports slow
- Published
The number of ships that have reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz has hit a record high, BBC Verify analysis of data from a UK maritime agency shows.
Twelve vessels were attacked between 5 and 11 October - the largest number of weekly strikes reported to the UK's Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency since the US-Israeli war with Iran began. The previous week saw 10 ships reporting attacks.
Six of the vessels were struck last Sunday, according to the UKMTO - a one-day high. So far this week, there have been four reported attacks.
As the number of strikes has risen, the recovery in oil shipments through the strait seen last month has slowed, industry data suggests.
BBC Verify collated incident reports published by the UKMTO on its website and created a timeline based on the first date cited in each report. This is approximate because some incidents use the date of the attack and some the date on which it was reported.
Experts say Tehran has been attacking ships in an effort to assert greater control over the waterway as the US military has increased the number of tankers it is shepherding through the south of the strait to evade Iranian strikes.
Iran is also carrying out more attacks on vessels further away from the Strait of Hormuz, according to experts.
The US military's Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, posted on social media that despite the attacks "commercial traffic continues to flow through the Strait of Hormuz with co-ordinated protection from US forces and regional partners".
Two crew missing after one of Sunday's attacks
The aftermath of one of Sunday's six reported attacks was captured in verified footage showing the Nicaragua-flagged tanker Petro Dolphin on fire, as filmed by the crew on a smaller boat nearby.
The vessel was struck by a drone close to the Sohar Anchorage, Oman, more than 250km (150 miles) from the strait, according to the maritime intelligence firm Vanguard.
Eleven Indian seafarers were rescued but two are still missing, the Forward Seamen's Union of India said.
Attacks have continued this week with the container ship GFS Pride sinking after a strike by an unknown projectile in the strait on Tuesday. Twenty-one crew were safely evacuated.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) published footage of what appeared to be the same ship sinking. It said the vessel was carrying "2,500 containers of contraband" and had taken an "unauthorised route".
Oil shipments stall
Middle East oil exports have slowed as the number of ship strikes has risen.
About 12.6 million barrels per day went through the strait on 13 October, below the 15 million reported at the end of September, data from trade intelligence firm Kpler shows. This compares with a pre-war baseline of some 17 million barrels per day.
The recent increase in attacks comes as US Navy data indicates the number of vessels given assistance to navigate the Strait of Hormuz during the first 10 days of October was up 85% compared with the same period in August.
Most of the oil being shipped from Gulf Arab states recently has been carried using a "shuttle" system where a fleet of tankers load up and sail through the strait before transferring their cargo to larger tankers in the Gulf of Oman.
These shuttle ships use a route close to Oman's coastline. Iran says this is "unauthorised" and insist vessels take an alternative route closer to its own shore.
So-called assisted transits were a key factor in helping drive oil flows from the Middle East back towards pre-war levels in September. This does not include Iranian exports which have completely stalled as a result of the US blockade of Iranian ports and ships.
Martin Kelly, CEO of Orbital Risk Intelligence, said Iran has "evolved its strategy" in response to this loosening of its control over the strait and has been carrying out "near daily or multiple attacks every single day".
"The aim here is to stop the ships going through and to deter others," he added.
The IRGC's navy has said strikes would not be "limited to the Strait of Hormuz" and later announced a "new deployment formation" across the region, according to state media.
Martin Kelly told BBC Verify that Iran is widening its attacks and targeting ships near the coast of Gulf Arab states and in the Gulf of Oman.
A tanker was struck by multiple projectiles north of Qatar on Thursday 8 October, more than 500km (310 miles) from the strait, resulting in multiple reported casualties, according to Vanguard.
Another tanker was attacked close to the UAE town of Al-Jazirah al-Hamra on Friday 9 October, Vanguard said.
Verified footage shows crew members running across the deck and putting on lifejackets as a large cloud of black smoke rises over the ship.
Additional reporting by Becky Dale
Graphics by Tom Shiel and Mark Edwards

title: Fed's Warsh says AI path will be 'very bumpy' but ultimately 'very good' for wealth
titleJa: Fed's Warsh says AI path will be 'very bumpy' but ultimately 'very good' for wealth
summaryJa: Warsh said he's optimistic that AI will make economies that use it well more productive and wealthier, warning the road there will be "very bumpy."
bodyOriginal:
BANGKOK — Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said he's optimistic that artificial intelligence will make economies that use it well more productive and wealthier, though he warned the road there will be "very bumpy" and its near-term effect on jobs is unknown.
Warsh spoke at a fireside chat with the International Monetary Fund's managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, as part of the weeklong IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok on Friday.
"I want you to hear from me optimism, but optimism leavened by the seriousness of purpose," Warsh said. A decade from now, he said, people will look back "and say this was hugely consequential."
The Fed raised rates to a range of 3.75% to 4% last month, its first hike since 2023. A communication blackout period starts later Friday, ahead of its Oct. 27-28 meeting.
Warsh also said the global economy has "broadly conformed" to the central bank's expectations since its September rate increase, but he declined to say what he will do at the coming meeting. "I don't prejudge meetings," he said.
Traders see a 72.3% chance for the Fed to keep the interest rate unchanged, according to CME Fed Watch, while the majority expect a 25 basis point hike at the December meeting.

title: Hybe shares jump 10% as K-pop sensation BTS' tour lifts earnings hopes
titleJa: Hybe shares jump 10% as K-pop sensation BTS' tour lifts earnings hopes
summaryJa: BTS' world tour and rising global demand for newer K-pop acts are fueling earnings expectations, sending Hybe shares soaring.
bodyOriginal:
Shares of Hybe, the company behind K-pop supergroup BTS, surged 10% on Friday as investors weighed an upbeat third-quarter earnings outlook fueled by its artistes' global concerts.
Hybe's third-quarter revenue is expected to reach 1.5 trillion won ($1.11 billion), up 106% from a year earlier, while operating profit is projected at 172.2 billion won, according to local brokerage firm iM Securities. Concert revenue is expected to come in at 717 billion won, nearly tripling from a year earlier.
The share price gain on Friday outperformed the broader Kospi, which rose 2.9%.
BTS' ongoing world tour featured 16 stadium shows in North America and eight in Europe during the third quarter.
Thiat, alongside expanding tours by newer acts including Enhypen, Katseye and Cortis, helped drive concert attendance to nearly 3 million during the quarter, potentially marking a quarterly record for the company, the report said.
Western markets accounted for more than 70% of total concert attendance for the first time, reflecting Hybe's growing international reach as its newer artistes expand their presence in North America and Europe, according to the report. Despite currency headwinds, concert, merchandise and licensing revenues are expected to reach record levels.
Concert margin outlook
While higher royalty payments to established artistes and initial touring costs for newer groups are expected to weigh on margins, the brokerage forecasts Hybe to maintain a double-digit operating margin, supported by the scale of BTS' world tour.
CGS Securities analyst Jiwoo Oh told CNBC after Hybe's second-quarter earnings that while concerts and appearances carry steeper costs for the company due to higher revenue sharing with artistes, merchandise, content and fan club businesses help boost the companies bottom line significantly.
She also pointed out that in its second quarter, Hybe delivered an 11.8% operating margin in the second quarter of 2026, with artist-direct revenue accounting for 72% of total sales and concerts alone accounting for 45% of total sales.
"We believe this demonstrates that stadium-scale operating leverage can more than offset the higher cost base associated with concerts," she added.
After Hybe reported second-quarter results on July 28, the company's shares crashed, wiping out as much as $1.96 billion in market cap in less than 24 hours.
Analysts said then that the sell-off was caused as profit margins missed expectations, despite revenue and operating profit reaching record highs, according to analysts.
Rookies step up
The iM Securities report said that the profitability of newer bands such as Katseye and Cortis in Western markets will be likely key to reducing the company's reliance on BTS, the report showed.
Still, stronger-than-expected demand for additional BTS concerts in Japan and the Middle East, as well as encore performances, could also lead to upward revisions to the company's 2027 earnings forecasts, iM Securities added.
Kyobo Securities, which expects third-quarter concert revenue to reach 724.4 billion won, expressed optimism around Hybe's newer acts, stating "growth among younger artists is becoming more visible alongside BTS' tour."
Cortis is selling around 600,000 albums per month on average, demonstrating strong fandom demand, the brokerage said, while Katseye is expanding its overseas presence on the back of global streaming and album performance.

title: Russia returns to G20 table in Bangkok on U.S. invitation that angers Europe
titleJa: Russia returns to G20 table in Bangkok on U.S. invitation that angers Europe
summaryJa: Russia’s return to the G20 table has tested how far Washington’s outreach to Moscow will strain ties with European allies.
bodyOriginal:
Russia's finance minister attended a Group of 20 meeting in Bangkok on Thursday, his second in-person appearance at the event since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, testing how far Washington's rapprochement with Moscow will strain ties with Europe.
Anton Siluanov and Bank of Russia Deputy Governor Elizaveta Danilova were listed as Russia's delegates at the finance ministers and central bank governors' meetings on the sidelines of the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, according to a seating plan seen by CNBC. Siluanov was in the meeting, according to a person familiar with the matter.
According to the layout document, Russian delegates were seated between attendees from South Korea and the United Arab Emirates.
German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil was also listed as an attendee. At the August G20 finance meeting in Asheville, North Carolina, he told Siluanov that Moscow must end the war and declined to pose in a group photo with him. The traditional group photo was ultimately taken without the Russian delegation after European officials protested.
Klingbeil has pushed back on the U.S. efforts to bring Russia back on to the international stage, reportedly saying after the Thursday meeting that "there will be no pretending that Russia is now returning as a normal member of the G20 and simply taking its seat at the table again — not with me, and not with the other Europeans."
Russia's seat at the table tests how far Washington can ease pressure on Moscow without breaking with its European allies. The U.S., which took over the G20 presidency this year, welcomed Russia's finance minister back to the finance talks after years of isolation over the invasion of Ukraine.
The Trump administration also introduced a deal to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel imports until April, drawing criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European allies. Dombrovskis told CNBC on Wednesday that "now it's not a time to ease sanctions on Russia."
In a statement issued after the Thursday meetings, Australian Treasurer Jim Chalmers said Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz and attacks on commercial vessels "must end." Those impacts "are exacerbated by Russia's unprovoked and unjustifiable war in Ukraine," he said, adding that Australia calls for Russia to end the war and respect Ukraine's sovereignty.
The finance chiefs ended the meeting without a joint communique, underscoring persistent divisions among members over the Middle East conflict, trade imbalances, and Russia's war with Ukraine. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who would normally chair the talks, skipped the meetings to stay in Washington.
The Asheville meeting also ended without a communique, after China objected to language on several issues, including efforts to rectify excessive global trade surpluses. The U.S. instead issued a chair's statement backed by every member present except China, with Bessent calling China "the dissenter."
Delegates started the day with a plated breakfast of baked goat cheese, spinach and egg soufflé with chutney made from locally grown Bijin tomatoes, according to a menu card at the venue. The bread basket came with "Nam Dok Mai" mango jam. Every card carried the U.S. presidency's stars-and-stripes G20 logo and its "Freedom 250" tagline, marking America's 250th anniversary.
The finance ministers' meeting Thursday could have helped lay the groundwork for improved coordination on a raft of global challenges, including energy problems stemming from the Middle East conflict and concerns about record public debt in advanced economies. Leaders are expected to convene at the next G20 summit in Miami in December.

title: Living with a stink? Technology might help
titleJa: Living with a stink? Technology might help
summaryJa: Smells from rubbish dumps and industrial facilities are being more carefully monitored.
bodyOriginal:
Living with a stink? Technology might help
- Published
Milpitas, an affluent city in California's Silicon Valley tech hub, has an odour problem.
For decades, residents have had to endure rank smells wafting from industrial sites, among them a 342-acre landfill.
"When I first moved here, I could not open my window for over 10 years," says Chia-Ling Kong, an engineer for a tech firm who lives around half a mile from the dump.
While things have got better in recent years, Kong says she and her neighbours must still contend with around "two or three hours of bad smells a day".
Perhaps befitting Silicon Valley, the community is putting its hopes in technology.
The operators of Newby Island landfill have been ordered by local authorities to use drones and install monitors to systematically track and measure the chemicals responsible for bad odours. They have also been told to automate the collection of landfill gases responsible for smells.
Kong is optimistic a data-driven approach will make a difference. "Hopefully with this continuous monitoring, it makes it easier to pinpoint problems at the moment it starts."
The operators of the landfill say they are committed to operating it safely and protecting air quality.
Just like in Milpitas, where Kong is part of a citizen's campaign against the odours, communities around the world are raising a stink about bad smells making day-to-day life miserable. Sometimes a rubbish dump is to blame, or it might be a sewage treatment works, or a reeking factory.
When the complaints start stacking up, resolving them is not always simple. Many countries have no regulations in place dictating how to manage smells.
In the US, for example, the Environmental Protection Agency does not regulate environmental odours as a pollutant. This leaves states and local governments to take charge of the issue.
Urban sprawl is often part of the problem, bringing communities closer to stinky facilities that may historically have been kept at a distance.
This is creating more demand for technologies to monitor and prevent smells. Odour consultant Micheal Bull says people are increasingly concerned about neighbourhood stinks.
"You're getting developments being built nearer to odorous processes… as land has become more valuable, there is also infilling," Bull says. He is speaking about his experiences in the UK, but it's a similar story in many parts of the world.
The technologies used to tackle industrial pongs generally fall into three categories: they absorb odours; convert them into something less smelly through a chemical reaction; or burn them away.
Experts on fixing industrial odours say that the best technologies, when used correctly, can remove 90% or more of the target compounds responsible for smells.
But this can be expensive and some operators opt for simpler and cheaper solutions. These include masking odours from landfill or sewage processing by spraying giant quantities of deodorisers.
Odour experts contacted for this article were dubious about the effectiveness of such industrial scale air fresheners. "In my view they're not likely to change the odours," says Bull, who likens them to fabric conditioner.
Bad smells from waste sites – a common cause of complaints – are among the stinkiest and most difficult to resolve, according to Carlos Diaz, an environmental consultant based in Spain. "Landfill is difficult to treat because you have a very large surface," he says.
In some places at least, technology is making a real difference. Residents in Des Moines, Iowa, have long complained of the so-called Eastside Funk, a putrid scent that residents report drifts over parts of the city.
A study commissioned by city authorities showed that a trio of industrial meat companies were among culprits.
"Within 10 miles, there's about half a million people," says Dalton Jacobus, who works in the Department of Neighborhood Services. "If the winds are out of the wrong direction, 100,000 people can be in the middle of that odour plume."
The authorities are now paying around $240,000 (£182,000) a year on technology to track the stink, so they can take action. "What we wanted to do was build a ring of odour monitors around the facilities that we suspected of emitting odours," says Jacobus.
The monitors, which measure levels of chemical compounds in the air, work in combination with a weather station to provide real-time data on the concentrations that are coming from each facility based off the wind patterns.
This has put an end to finger pointing about who's to blame each time a smell sparks complaints, says Jacobus. "Now we can say with reasonable certainty that 'this odour event did originate from your facility, what was going on'?"
Meanwhile, some of the sites that have been blamed for causing unpleasant smells in Des Moines have spent millions of dollars to upgrade their own odour control systems.
Smithfield Foods, which operates a meat processing in Des Moines, says it has invested $2m to install a regenerative thermal oxidiser that destroys the chemicals associated with bad smells. Even so, the company says it does not believe it is the source of odour complaints.
Before installing the monitors – which some local companies help pay for – officials in Des Moines would drive out to the source of a complaint to sniff the air.
Relying on the human nose to sniff out industrial smells is still commonplace. Claudia Barrios Obregón from Kunak, the company behind the monitors in Des Moines, says: "Right now, the way that cities control or measure odours is olfactometry: a human panel measures and gives an opinion of what the odour is like. But that's not that realistic."
The Spanish company's monitors are an example of so-called electronic noses that make it easier to detect smells.
Whatever technology is used, it can be hard to keep everyone happy, as smells are so subjective. "Unfortunately, the general rule is that the nastier we perceive the odour to be, the more sensitive towards it we are," says Johan Lundström, a professor in the science of smell at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, Sweden.

title: I find it quite demoralising in store - why I do all my shopping online
titleJa: I find it quite demoralising in store - why I do all my shopping online
summaryJa: After Primark announced plans for home delivery, we hear from women who never go into clothes stores.
bodyOriginal:
I find it quite demoralising in store - why I do all my shopping online
- Published
Jess Bacon does all her clothes shopping online.
As a plus-size woman, she finds the size ranges available in stores unreliable. "The sizing in store is notoriously bad. I find it quite demoralising in store," she says.
"The average size woman in the UK is a size 14 or a size 16. I think a lot of people just don't feel seen or represented," says the 29-year-old from Peterborough.
Jess, a culture journalist and author, finds shopping online "much quicker than going into a store, paying for parking, trying things on".
And she feels posting back items that don't fit is less hassle than returning in store, while frequent visits to her local post office give her "more of a community connection".
Jess notes Primark is one of the few High Street retailers where plus-size people can shop. In her experience, Primark stores usually stock up to a size 22.
But soon she'll have the option of staying home even for this - as, after years of holding out, Primark now plans to launch a home delivery service in Britain.
Even throughout the Covid-19 pandemic, when shops were closed, Primark didn't offer the ability to shop online. In 2022 it launched a click-and-collect service, but shoppers still had to travel for their purchases.
The retailer has not said when it expects to launch the service, but has bought a warehouse in Sheffield to enable it to ship products to homes.
Analysts say the decision shows Primark is facing major challenges from ultra-fast-fashion brands such as Shein.
Online shopping had been on the rise even before the surge seen during the pandemic.
Online accounted for 27.3% of all retail sales in August this year, according to the Office for National Statistics, up from 18.1% in August 2019.
Internet shopping has also been boosted by the decline of the High Street in many parts of the country, something which Jess has noticed in Peterborough. "We don't have John Lewis [anymore]. There's kind of not that much of a reason to go into town."
'I basically never go into clothes shops'
Like Jess, Julia Mitchell, who lives near Chichester, doesn't enjoy in-person clothes shopping. She finds it overstimulating and thinks there are better bargains to be had online.
"I basically never go into them [clothes shops]. It's not really something I enjoy," the 32-year-old says.
"I guess some people might be able to see stuff and pick it up and look at it, but for me, being able to get the best price is more important."
Julia, a content creator, tries to shop ethically and most of her purchases are second hand from Vinted.
The one thing she never shops online for, though, is books. "The thing about bookshops is that they are cultural spaces and community spaces."
Sandra Davies does all her shopping online. She has had three strokes and finds walking to and around stores too much physically.
"I've tried it on two occasions but on both times, standing in a queue for over 10 minutes was too much for me and I collapsed."
The 61-year-old from Sheffield says waiting for deliveries can be taxing as well, as she worries about missing the postie and having to reschedule.
Returns policy can 'make or break'
Julie Palmer, a retail analyst, is not surprised that Primark has finally moved into home deliveries as it has evidently recognised that "online sales bring scale".
However, she says a shop's returns policy for online purchases can "make or break" it. Many brands offer hassle-free returns, which Palmer says Primark must match in order to compete.
"Shoppers want them to be free, simple and quick. That means a generous window, lots of drop-off options and refunds that land within days, not weeks.
"When a policy is clunky or slow, customers remember it and shop elsewhere next time."
But returns are expensive for retailers. Some, like Asos, have started charging a fee if customers make frequent returns.
This is a balancing act, Palmer says, "because a fee can easily push a customer to a competitor".
"Most retailers that charge still offer free returns in store, which is a deliberate way to get people through the door and hopefully spending again."

title: Netflix Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria is leaving, will be replaced by Peter Rice
titleJa: Netflix Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria is leaving, will be replaced by Peter Rice
summaryJa: Netflix announced Bela Bajaria will be replaced by former Disney exec Peter Rice as the company's chief content officer.
bodyOriginal:
Netflix on Thursday announced Bela Bajaria will be replaced as the company's chief content officer by former Disney exec Peter Rice, effective Oct. 26.
Rice most recently oversaw Disney's cable channels, news programming and coverage of major sporting events.
"Peter is one of the most effective at-scale operators in the entertainment industry," co-CEO Ted Sarandos said in a statement. "I'm excited to welcome him to Netflix as Chief Content Officer as we continue to scale and deliver members more of the stories they love."
Before Rice was at Disney, he held roles at 21st Century Fox and Fox Searchlight Pictures. Netflix in its announcement called him "one of the entertainment industry's most respected creative executives." In his new role, Rice will oversee the company's global content organization, including scripted and unscripted series, film and live events.
"[Netflix has] shown again and again that they're willing to take chances on distinctive voices and fresh ideas, and I'm excited to work with the team to help bring even more great stories to members everywhere," he said in a statement.
Bajaria, who is leaving Netflix after nearly 10 years, most recently led the company's global content team. She had been focused on the company's live sports strategy, looking to create events out of buzzy games and tournaments.
"I'm incredibly grateful for everything she's done to help Netflix entertain the world," Sarandos said in a statement.
The announcement comes a day after Netflix instituted layoffs across its organization, eliminating approximately 6% of its workforce, or roughly 1,000 jobs. Shares of the company are down more than 20% this year, though the stock remained relatively unchanged in extended trading Thursday.
The media company will report its next quarterly earnings on Tuesday.

title: KFC to switch to Coca-Cola beverages in U.S. restaurants for the first time in decades
titleJa: KFC to switch to Coca-Cola beverages in U.S. restaurants for the first time in decades
summaryJa: KFC is switching from PepsiCo to Coca-Cola as its beverage supplier for U.S. restaurants.
bodyOriginal:
KFC's U.S. restaurants will ditch PepsiCo and switch to Coca-Cola beverages next year, marking the first time in decades that the Yum Brands chain has changed its drink supplier, the restaurant company said Thursday.
Some of KFC's international markets serve Coke products, but the chain's U.S. restaurants have stuck with PepsiCo drinks ever since Pepsi bought KFC in 1986. At the time of the acquisition, KFC was Coke's second-largest fountain account, trailing only McDonald's. Pepsi later spun off KFC, along with sister chains Pizza Hut and Taco Bell — but even as the combined Yum Brands, the company stayed loyal to its previous owner. Without Pepsi, Taco Bell would not serve its iconic Mountain Dew Baja Blast.
The change comes as KFC aims to win back U.S. diners, who have ditched the fried chicken chain for rivals such as Chick-fil-A or Popeyes.
"This decision is a critical step in the Kentucky Fried Comeback," KFC U.S. President Catherine Tan-Gillespie wrote in a memo to franchisees and employees obtained by CNBC. "A new beverage offering, with a new partner in Coca-Cola, gives us a platform to innovate, meet changing tastes and give customers more reasons to choose us."
For many fast-food chains, beverages have become a critical way to attract consumers. A number of restaurants, including McDonald's and Taco Bell, have broadened their drink offerings with options such as refreshers or "dirty soda." For its part, KFC recently unveiled new drinks, including iced coffees and shakes, at Open House, its innovation restaurant in McKinney, Texas.
Coke told CNBC earlier this year that the company has helped many of its restaurant partners create new drinks.
KFC expects to be pouring Coke beverages in all of its U.S. restaurants by the end of the first quarter of 2027, Tan-Gillespie said.
Tan-Gillespie also said that Pepsi remains an important partner for KFC's parent company and the chain's international markets.
For decades, Coke and Pepsi have tussled over important restaurant partners, which represent both a sales opportunity and the chance to grow the visibility of their beverage brands.
It is unusual for large restaurant chains to switch beverage providers, but not unprecedented. In 2024, Pepsi poached Subway, the largest U.S. restaurant chain by number of locations, from Coke. Besides KFC, Coke has wooed away a number of notable Pepsi customers in recent years, including Culver's, Arby's and Panda Express.

title: Porsche reveals Mission S concept car that previews new design identity
titleJa: Porsche reveals Mission S concept car that previews new design identity
summaryJa: Porsche revealed a concept car called Mission S as part of a turnaround plan that includes efforts to boost profits through higher-end products and lower sales.
bodyOriginal:
Porsche on Thursday revealed a concept car called Mission S that signals a new design direction and flagship model for the famed German sports carmaker.
The debut of the sleek midengine vehicle is part of a turnaround plan revealed last week by the Volkswagen-controlled brand that includes efforts to boost profits through higher-end products and lower vehicle sales.
Porsche described Mission S as "a first glimpse of the brand's evolved design identity" that also represents a "super sports car platform" that will be positioned above its iconic 911 sports car.
The vehicle's design is recognizably Porsche but with more aggressive styling compared with its current models, including new hood vents and a roof scoop. Its rear features more differentiated flair in which the vehicle's spoiler flows into its rear panels.
"A Porsche must be recognisable as a Porsche at first glance," Porsche Chairman Michael Leiters said in a release. "The Mission S provides a glimpse of the ideas and design features that will shape Porsche in the coming years."
Automakers routinely use concept vehicles to gauge customer interest, showcase future technologies and signal the direction of a vehicle or brand.
The company did not release expected pricing or performance specifications for such future models. Starting prices for its current 911 models range from roughly $135,500 for an entry-level Carrera to more than $203,000 for a Carrera 4 GTS convertible.
During Porsche's capital markets day on Oct. 7, the company outlined its "Sportwagenschmiede '35" turnaround plan, which focuses on emphasizing high-end sports cars and luxury SUVs to get the carmaker back on track.
Porsche's operating margin last year was only 1.1%, compared with 14.1% in 2024, as the company deals with increased costs, U.S. tariffs and declining sales in China.
The turnaround plan includes a long-term target for a group operating margin of 15% and a midterm breakeven point of 200,000 units or below annually. That compares with sales of 279,449 in 2025.

title: CoreWeave credit default swaps hit distress levels as investors sour on AI debt
titleJa: CoreWeave credit default swaps hit distress levels as investors sour on AI debt
summaryJa: CoreWeave's credit stress continued to spiral on Thursday amid a broader sell-off in AI-related names.CoreWeave — a so-called neocloud company — has taken on more than $51 billion of debt and obligations to finance its AI infrastructure buildout. It's now facing a rebellion from stock and bond investors as concerns mount about AI overspending and debt levels.
bodyOriginal:
CoreWeave's credit stress continued to spiral on Thursday amid a broader sell-off in AI-related names.
CoreWeave — a so-called neocloud company — has taken on more than $51 billion of debt and obligations to finance its AI infrastructure buildout. It's now facing a rebellion from stock and bond investors as concerns mount about AI overspending and debt levels.
Yields on CoreWeave debt have continued to climb, with the yield to maturity on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 reaching 15.78%. Bond yields move inversely to prices. Meanwhile, the spread on its five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, at one point soared above 1,140 basis points. It last stood at nearly 1,038 bps — a 16% week-over-week jump and 164% higher than a year ago.
Credit concerns are spreading into AI equities too. CoreWeave's stock dropped during trading Thursday before recovering and closing 5.94% higher. The moved followed Wednesday's 15.5% nosedive.
Other neocloud stocks were under similar pressure. Nebius also sank before climbing higher to close 1.29% and and Iren ultimately ended the day down less than 1%.
Anxiety about AI overspending is also spreading. For instance, shares of Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices sold off following a big sell-off in South Korean chip stocks. Micron closed up 1.87%, while AMD fell 1.5%.
While AI debt worries have been rising steadily, investors have suddenly grown skittish about the underlying finances of companies borrowing heavily to buy chips, build data centers, and rent out computing power.
Coreweave's credit default swaps are one place to see that stress.
Credit default swaps are contracts where buyers pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. The spread widening in CoreWeave's CDS means investors view the debt as riskier.
The market is "basically saying 'no mas' to AI debt without operating cash flow support," the Evercore ISI trading desk said.
A spread level of 1,000 basis points or above is generally a sign of credit distress, said Gavan Nolan, executive director of fixed income pricing at S&P Global Market Intelligence.
No one is questioning whether demand for CoreWeave's services is real, since the company has contracts with all the big hyperscalers, Nolan said. The question is whether the cash flows will ultimately arrive.
"It's obviously heavily negative free cash flow at the moment, and it needs that cash flow to arrive really to justify all the capex that it's spending," Nolan said.
'Self-fulfilling prophecy'
CEO Mike Intrator dismissed the market moves on Wednesday, according to a memo obtained by CNBC.
"When you are building a new type of technology company there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally," he wrote. "We are confident in our backlog which more than supports all of our debt obligations."
The backlog is over $100 billion, with around two-thirds of it with investment-grade counterparts including Microsoft, Meta, IBM and Caterpillar, Deutsche Bank said in a note Thursday. The firm reiterated its buy-rating on the stock Wednesday, calling the dislocation a buying opportunity.
"The problem is this kind of concern can prove to be a self-fulfilling prophecy, and risks triggering broader issues in other AI-related names," said Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research.
Domino effects may already be happening. Oracle's five-year CDS spread also spiked this week. It was last at 282 basis points, a roughly 10% increase in one week.
"A downgrade from its BBB rating would risk pressuring IG-only investors into forced sales," Reid said.
